abstract: |
  Carbon taxes stall where coal dominates power or where industry competes abroad, because the tax charges producers for every tonne they still emit, not only for the tonnes they could avoid. A revenue-neutral feebate charges producers above a sector benchmark of emissions per unit of output and rebates those below it. It gives the same incentive to switch as a tax at the same rate but leaves average costs almost unchanged. In a stylized coal-heavy grid at \$50 per tonne, a tax raises average generation cost by 87 percent; a feebate raises it by nothing at the outset. Governments should use feebates where carbon taxes stall.

*Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated.*

# Executive summary {.unnumbered}

*The problem.* A carbon tax sends two signals. The relative-price signal makes coal dearer than gas and gas dearer than solar, and it does the abating. The average-cost signal charges every producer for every tonne it still emits, and it does the political damage. In coal-heavy power the average-cost signal is extreme: \$50 per tonne of CO₂ nearly triples the price of coal bought at \$2.50 per gigajoule, while it raises gas by a third. In trade-exposed industry it hands market share to untaxed competitors. Governments respond by exempting the sectors that emit most or by holding the rate down for everyone.

*The proposal.* Price these sectors with a feebate. Each producer pays $t(e_i - \bar e)$ per unit of output: a fee when its emissions intensity $e_i$ is above the sector benchmark $\bar e$, a rebate when it is below. With the benchmark at the sector average, fees fund rebates exactly. Output-based rebating of a carbon tax is the same instrument seen from the tax side.

*Why it works.* Every tonne avoided is worth $t$ to the producer, as under a tax, so the switch from coal to gas and renewables is the same. But the average producer pays nothing net. In a stylized grid that is 60 percent coal, a \$50 tax raises average generation cost by \$32 per megawatt-hour, or 87 percent. The feebate raises it by nothing at the outset and afterwards only by the resource cost of the switch. Power stays cheap while transport and heating electrify, and coal incumbents pay for their clean competitors. In industry the feebate leaves exporters' average costs, and so their market share, almost untouched.

*The evidence.* Sweden's refunded charge on nitrogen oxides cut emission rates at large combustion plants by 40 percent in six years, at a charge level its analysts judged out of reach for a tax. France's car bonus-malus shifted sales sharply but cost the budget €285 million in its first year because the benchmark did not move with sales. Canada's output-based pricing for industry survived the 2025 removal of its consumer carbon charge.

*What it costs.* A feebate raises no revenue and does not discourage use of the product, so it buys fewer tonnes per dollar of carbon price than a tax. The IMF puts feebate and regulation packages at 50–70 percent of a tax's emission cuts. A consumption charge restores the demand margin. Benchmarks need facility data and protection from lobbying.

*What to do.* Coal-heavy countries should replace planned carbon taxes on power with a feebate per megawatt-hour, benchmarked to the grid average, updated every year and written into law. They should run the same instrument for steel, cement and aluminum. Importing jurisdictions should credit feebates at the border, and development lenders should finance the transition they create.

# 1. A carbon tax charges the whole bill, not just the margin

A carbon tax at rate $t$ does two separate things. It raises the cost of dirty production relative to clean, which is what cuts emissions. It also charges each producer $t$ on every tonne it still emits, which raises the sector's average cost and transfers the carbon bill to the treasury. The first effect is the policy. The second is a side effect, and it decides whether the policy survives.

The side effect concentrates losses on organized groups, which is why it is fatal. Costs concentrated on a few identifiable firms and diffuse benefits are the recipe for successful opposition [@Olson1965]. Canada shows the pattern: it removed its consumer fuel charge on 1 April 2025 and kept its industrial output-based system, which charges only emissions above a benchmark [@FinanceCanada2025; @OBPSRegs].

A feebate keeps the first effect and drops the second. A producer with emissions intensity $e_i$, in tonnes of CO₂ per unit of output, pays $t(e_i - \bar e)$ per unit, where $\bar e$ is the sector's benchmark. Above the benchmark it pays a fee; below, it receives a rebate. Set $\bar e$ at the output-weighted sector average and fees equal rebates. Each tonne avoided is still worth $t$, so the incentive to cut intensity is identical to a tax. The sector's average price rises only by the resource cost of abatement, which in the series' benchmark model is $\tfrac12 t\,\Delta e$, half the rate times the cut in intensity [@CFPB11]. Output-based rebating, a carbon tax whose revenue is returned per unit of output, is the same instrument [@Fischer2001; @SternerHoglund2000].

# 2. Power: keep electricity cheap while coal leaves

Coal is where a carbon tax bites hardest, because coal is cheap per unit of energy and rich in carbon. Other bituminous coal emits 94.6 kg of CO₂ per gigajoule and natural gas 56.1 kg [@IPCC2006]. At stylized prices of \$2.50 per gigajoule for coal and \$8 for gas, a \$50 tax adds \$4.73 to coal, a 189 percent rise, and \$2.81 to gas, 35 percent. Diesel at \$1 a liter rises 13 percent. Because a carbon tax must be uniform per tonne, the rate a coal-dependent economy can bear sets the rate for everything else.

A feebate gives coal, gas and solar the same relative costs as the tax while leaving the average untouched. Table 1 and Figure 1 show a stylized grid that is 60 percent coal, 20 percent gas and 20 percent solar, with an average intensity of 0.64 tCO₂/MWh. At \$50 per tonne the tax raises coal's cost by \$47 per MWh and gas by \$18, so solar beats both and gas beats coal. The feebate charges coal \$15, rebates gas \$14 and solar \$32. The gaps between technologies are the same \$29, \$47 and \$18 under both instruments, so dispatch and investment respond identically. The difference is the average: the tax adds \$32 per MWh to a system that cost \$37, an 87 percent rise in generation cost; the feebate adds nothing.

| Stylized power system, \$50/tCO₂ | Coal | Gas | Solar | System average |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Emissions intensity (tCO₂/MWh) | 0.95 | 0.37 | 0 | 0.64 |
| Generation cost before policy (\$/MWh) | 30 | 55 | 40 | 37 |
| Carbon tax: change in cost (\$/MWh) | +47 | +18 | 0 | +32 |
| Feebate, benchmark 0.64: change (\$/MWh) | +15 | −14 | −32 | 0 |
| Feebate after the shift, benchmark 0.45 (\$/MWh) | +25 | −4 | −23 | +2 |

"After the shift" assumes a fifth of output moves from coal to solar, so the mix is 40/20/40; the +\$2 is the resource cost of that switch.

![Change in generation cost per MWh at \$50/tCO₂ under a carbon tax and a revenue-neutral feebate, stylized grid of 60 percent coal, 20 percent gas and 20 percent solar. Both give the same cost gaps between technologies; only the tax raises the system average. Generated by figures/make_figures.py.](figures/fig1-power-tax-vs-feebate.png){width=100%}

The benchmark falls as the grid cleans, so the feebate tightens on laggards by itself. When a fifth of output moves from coal to solar, the average intensity falls to 0.45 and the rebate per MWh from \$32 to \$23. Coal's net charge rises from \$15 to \$25 per MWh even though the rate has not changed, and it approaches the full \$47 as the benchmark approaches zero. The feebate converges on a carbon tax without a single vote to raise the rate. The power price meanwhile rises only by the resource cost of the switch, \$2 per MWh here, and never by more than $t$ times the fall in average intensity, because no generator abates a tonne that costs more than $t$.

Cheap power matters because electricity is the clean energy carrier for everything else. In the International Energy Agency's net-zero pathway, electricity's share of final energy rises from 20 percent in 2020 to nearly 50 percent in 2050 [@IEA2021]. A tax that raises generation costs by 87 percent, as in Table 1, makes the clean carrier dearer just as households and firms decide whether to buy heat pumps and electric vehicles.

Power also holds the capital stock that must turn over first. Existing energy infrastructure would emit about 658 GtCO₂ over its life if operated as in the past, more than half of it in electricity, and the cheapest early retirements are in electricity and industry [@Tong2019]. A feebate pays for this turnover inside the sector: the fees of coal plants fund the rebates of clean entrants, and the earliest movers earn the most. Generators respond to relative prices: the UK's Carbon Price Support, a top-up carbon tax on generators, cut power-sector emissions by 20.5–26 percent a year over 2013–2017 as coal plants ran less and closed sooner [@Leroutier2022]. A feebate at the same rate preserves that relative price. The IMF describes the same instrument for power, a fee or rebate in proportion to output times the gap between a generator's emission rate and the industry average [@IMF2019].

# 3. Industry: competitiveness, rebating and the border

In trade-exposed industry a feebate removes the competitiveness cost of carbon pricing. A tax raises the average cost of every tonne of steel a country makes, and untaxed imports and rival exporters take the market. A feebate raises it only by the resource cost of abatement. In the series' stylized steel sector, at \$50 per tonne of CO₂, a feebate raises the price by \$15 per tonne of steel and a tax by \$85 [@CFPB11]. Modeling of the United States, Canada and Europe finds that output-based rebating for key manufacturing sectors achieves many of the gains of full border adjustment [@FischerFox2012].

The cost is that a feebate subsidizes output. Because the rebate is paid per unit, it gives up the incentive to use less of the product, and a pure intensity standard can even raise emissions [@HollandHughesKnittel2009; @Fischer2001]. The remedy is a separate charge on consumption: output-based rebating plus a consumption tax on the same goods is equivalent to border carbon adjustment [@BohringerRosendahlStorrosten2017]. That is the series' two-track design: a feebate prices what a country makes, and a carbon component of VAT prices what it consumes, imports included [@CFPB11; @CFPB16]. Where producers have market power, as in cement, output-based allocation can also offset the output losses that market power causes [@FowlieReguantRyan2016].

Border measures do not yet credit feebates. The EU border mechanism reduces an importer's liability only for a carbon price effectively paid in the country of origin, net of rebates [@EU2023, Art. 9]. Under a feebate the average exporter pays nothing net, so it earns little or no deduction. Exporters still gain because the border charge falls with verified embodied emissions, which the feebate cuts. The fix is to recognize a feebate's carbon-price equivalent, the tax rate that would cut emissions as much, rather than cash paid [@CFPB13; @CFPB17].

# 4. Evidence from feebates in use

Sweden's charge on nitrogen oxides is the clearest test of a production feebate. From 1992 large combustion plants paid 40 kronor per kilogram of NOx, about \$5,000 per tonne, and almost all revenue was returned in proportion to useful energy produced [@SternerHoglund2000]. Mean emission rates at the roughly 200 plants first covered fell 40 percent by 1998, administration cost 0.2–0.3 percent of revenue, and within every sector some firms were net payers and others net recipients. The authors judged that a tax at that rate would not have been politically feasible [@SternerHoglund2000; @SternerIsaksson2006]. The refund sped adoption of post-combustion abatement [@Bonilla2015], and the median plant caught up with best practice as the best cut emissions by about 70 percent [@SternerTurnheim2009].

France's vehicle bonus-malus shows what happens when the benchmark does not move. From January 2008 buyers of cars below 130 gCO₂/km received up to €1,000 (€5,000 for electric cars) and buyers above 160 g paid up to €2,600. Class B cars rose from 20 percent of sales at the end of 2007 to nearly 50 percent in early 2009. The scheme was calibrated to be budget-neutral but cost the state about €285 million in 2008, and the government cut the rebates in 2010 [@DHaultfoeuille2014]. Because the scheme also raised car sales, @DHaultfoeuille2014 estimate its overall effect on emissions as negative; a later structural model finds a 1.6 percent cut in average CO₂ emissions [@Durrmeyer2022].

Canada's output-based pricing system is a feebate tilted to raise revenue. Since 2019 facilities pay on emissions above an output-based standard set at 80, 90 or 95 percent of the national production-weighted average intensity, depending on leakage risk, and earn tradable credits below it [@OBPSRegs; @CanadaGazette2022]. From 2023 most standards tighten by 2 percent a year and the most exposed by 1 percent, while the national carbon price rises from C\$65 to C\$170 per tonne in 2030 [@CanadaGazette2022]. For new gas-fired generation the standard falls from 370 tCO₂e per GWh in 2021 to zero in 2030 [@OBPSRegs], a published path of the kind this brief recommends.

# 5. Design

**Set the benchmark at the output-weighted average of last year's actual intensities, and update it every year.** That keeps the scheme revenue-neutral after the event, which is where France failed. A benchmark below the average, as in Canada, raises revenue; one above it pays a net subsidy and expands output. A statutory formula, or a published declining path, protects the benchmark from lobbying.

**Use one benchmark per product, not per fuel.** A benchmark for coal plants and another for gas plants would remove the coal-to-gas signal that does most early abatement. If stranded coal assets must be compensated, pay a time-limited transfer tied to closures, and end it within a few years.

**Decide who shares the rebate.** Rebating existing hydro and nuclear output pays windfalls without changing behavior; Sweden kept nuclear plants out of its refund pool [@SternerHoglund2000]. Restricting rebates to fossil plants and new clean capacity concentrates the money on the switch.

**Combine usage and purchase feebates.** A usage feebate, per megawatt-hour or per tonne of steel, prices how existing plants run and what replaces them, which is what power and industry need. A purchase feebate prices a durable choice once, as France does for cars, and suits vehicles and boilers, whose use is hard to meter.

**Verify at the facility.** Power plants already meter fuel and output, and steel, cement and aluminum plants exporting to the EU now measure embodied emissions for the border mechanism [@EU2023]. Size thresholds keep small emitters out at first; Sweden lowered its threshold from 50 to 25 GWh a year in 1996–97 [@SternerHoglund2000].

**Plan the revenue and the legal text.** A feebate funds nothing, so pair it with revenue-raising taxes on transport fuels, or lower the benchmark over time; once $\bar e$ reaches zero the feebate is a carbon tax. In traded goods the rebate needs drafting care under World Trade Organization subsidy rules [@Trachtman2017].

# 6. What to do

Finance ministries and energy regulators in coal-heavy countries should legislate a power-sector feebate at the rate they would have wanted for a carbon tax, levied per tonne and rebated per megawatt-hour against the grid-average benchmark, with the benchmark recomputed annually by formula. They should run the same instrument for steel, cement, aluminum and fertilizer, benchmarked per tonne of product, and add the consumption charge of Brief 1.6 when the VAT system can carry it. The EU and other importers should credit feebates at the border on a carbon-price-equivalent basis. Development banks should lend against the predictable rebate stream that clean entrants will earn, which lowers the cost of replacing coal.
